title: Harvest animal products: animal products systems

lessons.title: Animal product systems and the value chain
lessons.html:
What counts as an animal product system

An animal product system is everything from the live animal on the farm to the product a buyer pays for. In South Africa the main systems are red meat (beef, mutton, goat), pork, poultry meat and eggs, milk, wool and mohair, hides and skins, honey and game products. Each has its own harvesting method, quality standards and buyers, and a manager must plan harvesting as part of the whole enterprise, not as an afterthought.

Steps common to every system

  1. Plan the harvest: timing, numbers, labour, equipment and the market or contract.
  2. Prepare the animals: correct condition, health status, withdrawal periods for any remedy completed as per the label or vet.
  3. Harvest: milking, shearing, egg collection, or sending animals for slaughter at a registered abattoir.
  4. Handle and store: cool, clean, dry and traceable.
  5. Grade and market: sort by quality class so you are paid for what you produce.

Legal and market framework

Slaughter for sale must take place at an abattoir registered under the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000. Animal welfare during handling and transport falls under the Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962. Buyers increasingly ask for traceability, so keep animal identification and movement records for every batch.

Consider a mixed farm in the Eastern Cape running Dohne Merino sheep and a small beef herd. Its products are wool (shearing once a year or twice for shorter staple), lambs to the abattoir and weaners to a feedlot. Each product has a different calendar, and good planning stops shearing, weaning and lambing from clashing for the same labour and kraal space.

lessons.title: Harvesting milk, fibre and eggs
lessons.html:
Products harvested from the live animal

Milk

Milk quality is judged mainly on hygiene (bacterial count), somatic cell count (a sign of mastitis), composition (butterfat and protein) and freedom from residues. A good milking routine is: calm cows, fore-strip and check the first milk, clean and dry teats, attach units promptly, avoid over-milking, post-dip teats, and cool milk quickly in a clean bulk tank. Milk from cows treated with antibiotics must be kept out of the tank for the full withholding period on the label or as your vet directs.

Wool and mohair

Shearing is planned around weather, lambing and the staple length buyers want. Shear sheep dry and empty (kept off feed for some hours as advised by your shearing contractor) on a clean board. Skirt the fleece to remove belly wool, stains and locks, then class it into lines by fineness, length and style so it fits the broker's grading. Keep plastic baling twine and other contaminants away from the shed, because foreign fibre lowers the price of the whole clip.

Eggs

Collect eggs at least twice a day, more often in hot weather. Remove dirty, cracked and misshapen eggs. Store clean eggs cool, pointed end down, and rotate stock so the oldest leave first. Record lay percentage daily; a sudden drop can signal disease, a feed or water problem, or stress.

Measuring performance

ProductKey measure
MilkLitres per cow per day, butterfat and protein, cell count
WoolClean yield, fibre diameter in microns, staple length
EggsLay percentage, grade-out of saleable eggs

lessons.title: Preparing animals for slaughter and adding value
lessons.html:
Meat, hides and value adding

Preparing slaughter stock

Carcass value depends on the animal's age, fatness and conformation, and on how it was handled before slaughter. In the South African carcass classification system, age is shown by a letter based on teeth and fat cover by a number; buyers pay different prices for different classes, so know what your market wants before you finish animals.

  • Select animals at the right weight and fat cover for the contract.
  • Check that every withdrawal period for dips, doses and injections is complete. Follow the product label or your vet; never guess.
  • Handle quietly. Stress and bruising before slaughter cause dark-cutting meat and trimmed carcasses that lose money.
  • Load at the correct density, provide water, and use a roadworthy vehicle with non-slip flooring.
  • Send the correct identification and movement documents with the load.

Hides and skins

Hides are damaged by ticks, brand marks in the wrong place, wire scratches and poor salting or drying. Good tick control and careful handling on the farm add value at the tannery.

Value adding

Some farms add value by processing on farm: cheese, yoghurt, biltong or spun mohair. This can raise income, but it brings new requirements: a registered facility, food safety systems, labelling and marketing effort. Do a budget comparing the extra income with the extra cost and risk before you invest.

Safety

Loading ramps, crushes and shearing sheds carry injury risks. Never stand behind or in the escape path of cattle in a race, use guarded shearing equipment and isolate power before working on machines.

Key points

  • Plan harvesting as part of the whole enterprise calendar.
  • Product quality is made on the farm: hygiene, handling, residue control.
  • Always complete withdrawal periods as stated on the label or by your vet.
  • Calm handling prevents bruising and dark-cutting meat.
  • Grade and class products so you are paid for quality.
